title: Menopause: diagnosis and hormone replacement therapy
subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
summary: Diagnose perimenopause and menopause clinically at 45 or over without FSH testing. Offer HRT for vasomotor symptoms (combined oestrogen and progestogen if a uterus is present, transdermal oestrogen if VTE risk is raised), vaginal oestrogen for genitourinary symptoms, and review at 3 months then yearly.

sections.title: Diagnosis
items: Age 45 or over with symptoms, no tests needed: perimenopause if vasomotor symptoms have recently started with any change in the menstrual cycle; menopause if no period for at least 12 months (not on hormonal contraception), or by symptoms after hysterectomy.
At 45 or over do not use AMH, inhibin, oestradiol, antral follicle count or ovarian volume. Do not use FSH in women taking combined hormonal contraception or high-dose progestogen.
Consider serum FSH only at age 40 to 45 with symptoms and a change in cycle, or under 40 when menopause is suspected.
Premature ovarian insufficiency (under 40): symptoms with absent or infrequent periods and raised FSH on 2 samples 4 to 6 weeks apart. Never diagnose on a single test; do not use AMH routinely.

Symptoms: hot flushes and night sweats, sleep disturbance, low mood or anxiety, reduced libido, joint aches, vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, urinary urgency and recurrent UTI. Some ethnic groups and people with lifelong conditions reach menopause earlier.

sections.title: Before starting treatment
items: Ask about VTE (personal and family), breast, endometrial or ovarian cancer, coronary disease, stroke, liver disease, migraine and unexplained vaginal bleeding; measure BP and BMI.
Unexplained postmenopausal or intermenstrual bleeding needs assessment for endometrial cancer before HRT.
Discuss contraception: HRT is not a contraceptive. FSRH advises contraception until 12 months after the last period if over 50, or 2 years if under 50.
Keep up to date with national breast and cervical screening.

sections.title: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT)
items: Offer HRT for vasomotor symptoms. With a uterus give combined HRT (oestrogen plus progestogen); after total hysterectomy give oestrogen-only HRT. Use the lowest effective dose.

Sequential combined HRT suits women still having periods; continuous combined HRT (no monthly bleed) is used after menopause and lowers endometrial cancer risk, whereas sequential HRT may slightly raise it.

Transdermal oestradiol (patch, gel, spray) does not increase VTE and is unlikely to raise stroke risk; oral oestrogen increases both. Prefer transdermal if VTE risk is raised, including BMI above 30 kg/m2.
Endometrial protection: micronised progesterone 200 mg at night for 12 days of each 28-day cycle (sequential) or 100 mg every night (continuous), or a 52 mg LNG-IUS.

Benefit-risk is most favourable when started under 60 or within 10 years of menopause; starting later carries higher absolute risks of coronary disease, stroke, VTE and dementia (The Menopause Society 2022).
Agree likely duration at the outset; there is no fixed stop date. Symptoms may return on stopping; tapering and stopping abruptly give the same longer-term outcome.
Consider HRT for low mood (not depression) starting with other menopausal symptoms, and testosterone (off-label) for low sexual desire if HRT alone is not effective.

sections.title: Genitourinary symptoms and non-hormonal options
items: Offer vaginal oestrogen (cream, gel, tablet, pessary or ring) for genitourinary symptoms, including in women already on systemic HRT. Absorption is minimal, serious harms are very rare, and no progestogen is needed.
Symptoms often return when vaginal oestrogen stops; it can continue long term with review. Moisturisers and lubricants can be used alone or with it.
If these fail or are not tolerated consider vaginal prasterone; oral ospemifene if local treatment is impractical. Do not offer vaginal laser outside trials.
Menopause-specific CBT helps vasomotor symptoms, sleep problems and low mood, with HRT or when HRT is contraindicated or declined.

Fezolinetant 45 mg orally once daily for moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms when HRT is unsuitable (NICE TA1143, 2026); check liver tests before starting and monthly for the first 3 months, then periodically.
Do not routinely offer SSRIs, SNRIs or clonidine first line for vasomotor symptoms alone.

sections.title: Review
items: Review each treatment at 3 months for effect and tolerability, then yearly; refer to a menopause specialist if symptoms persist or side effects continue.
Bleeding is common in the first 6 months of systemic HRT and within 3 months of a dose or preparation change; unscheduled bleeding beyond these times needs prompt assessment.

Re-discuss risks each year: breast cancer risk with combined HRT rises with duration (lower with sequential than continuous), falls after stopping but persists for at least 10 years; oestrogen-only HRT has little or no effect on breast cancer risk.
HRT reduces fragility fracture risk while taken. Stop systemic HRT if breast cancer is diagnosed.

sections.title: Special groups
items: Premature ovarian insufficiency: offer HRT or combined hormonal contraception until at least the usual age of natural menopause unless contraindicated (for example hormone-sensitive cancer). Early menopause (40 to 44): benefits and risks lie between POI and age 45 or over.

Personal history or high risk of breast cancer: refer to a menopause specialist. For genitourinary symptoms offer non-hormonal products first, then consider vaginal oestrogen; involve the oncologist if on an aromatase inhibitor.
High VTE risk (strong family history, thrombophilia): consider haematology advice before HRT. Previous coronary disease or stroke: HRT only via a clinician with menopause expertise.
Type 2 diabetes is not a contraindication; HRT does not raise diabetes risk or worsen glucose control.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Ordering FSH in women over 45 with typical symptoms, or in women on combined contraception.
Giving unopposed systemic oestrogen to a woman with a uterus (endometrial hyperplasia and cancer).
Prescribing HRT to prevent cardiovascular disease or dementia; NICE advises against both.
Withholding vaginal oestrogen because of warnings that apply to systemic HRT.
Assuming HRT provides contraception in perimenopause.

drugs.name: Oestradiol (oral)
drugs.notes: Oral route raises VTE and stroke risk; prefer transdermal if risk factors. Add a progestogen if a uterus is present.

drugs.name: Oestradiol (transdermal patch)
drugs.dose: 25 to 100 micrograms/24 hours, patch changed once or twice weekly by brand (50 micrograms/24 hours is a standard dose)
drugs.notes: Preferred with VTE risk, BMI above 30 kg/m2, migraine or malabsorption.

drugs.name: Micronised progesterone
drugs.dose: Sequential: 200 mg orally at bedtime for 12 days of each 28-day cycle. Continuous: 100 mg orally at bedtime daily
drugs.notes: Endometrial protection with oestrogen in women with a uterus.

drugs.name: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system
drugs.notes: Endometrial protection for the licensed duration and also contraception.

drugs.name: Vaginal oestradiol
drugs.dose: 10 microgram vaginal tablet daily for 2 weeks, then twice weekly
drugs.notes: Genitourinary symptoms; no progestogen needed. Can be used with systemic HRT.

drugs.name: Fezolinetant
drugs.notes: Non-hormonal option when HRT is unsuitable. Liver tests before starting, monthly for 3 months, then periodically; stop if liver injury.
